title: Bind Mounts & Tmpfs Mounts 🔗
description: Share directories between host and container and create in‑memory temporary filesystems.

slides.title: Bind Mounts – A Window to the Host 🪟
slides.content:
# Mount Any Host Directory

Unlike volumes, bind mounts map an arbitrary host directory (or file) into the container.

```bash
docker run -v /host/path:/container/path IMAGE
```

- Changes in the container are instantly visible on the host, and vice versa.
- The host path must exist (otherwise it’s created as a directory by Docker on Linux, but may behave differently on other OS).
- No Docker management – you control the directory.

**Ideal for:**
- Development with live code reloading.
- Sharing configuration files.
- Providing large datasets from the host.

slides.title: Bind Mount in Action ⚡
slides.content: Live code reload for a Node.js app:
slides.codeSnippet:
# Your source code is in /home/user/project
# The container expects code in /app

docker run -v /home/user/project:/app -p 3000:3000 node:18-alpine node /app/server.js

# Any changes in /home/user/project immediately affect the container

quizData.question: Which statement is true about bind mounts?

options.text: They are managed by Docker and stored in /var/lib/docker/volumes/
They map a specific host path into the container
They cannot be used in production
They persist after the container is removed, managed by Docker

quizData.explanation: Bind mounts directly use an existing host directory. Volumes are managed by Docker.

slides.title: Permissions & Portability Concerns ⚠️
slides.content:
# Beware of Bind Mount Pitfalls

- **File ownership**: UID/GID inside the container may not match the host, causing permission errors.
- **Portability**: The Dockerfile now depends on host paths; it won’t run on another machine without those paths.
- **Security**: The container can modify host files (unless mounted `ro`).

> In production, prefer named volumes for application data. Bind mounts are great for development and config injection.

slides.title: Tmpfs Mounts – In‑Memory Storage 🧠
slides.content:
# For Transient Sensitive Data

A tmpfs mount stores data in the host’s RAM (or swap), not on disk.

```bash
docker run --tmpfs /app/tmp alpine
# or with --mount:
docker run --mount type=tmpfs,destination=/app/tmp alpine
```

- Data is wiped when the container stops.
- Cannot be shared between containers.
- Useful for temporary files, caches, or secrets you don’t want on disk.

> No --read-only required; tmpfs is inherently volatile.

quizData.question: Data in a tmpfs mount persists across container restarts.
quizData.explanation: Tmpfs is temporary; it lives in memory and is destroyed when the container stops.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## The `--mount` vs `-v` for tmpfs
Use `--mount type=tmpfs,destination=/tmp,tmpfs-size=64m` to limit memory usage. The shorthand `--tmpfs` doesn't support size options directly (use `--tmpfs /tmp:rw,size=64m`).
